To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the majority of aquatic farmers in BCE Lake use OPs/CM pesticides, which are known for their acute toxicity.
50% (95% CI: 42–57%) of the pesticides used by the farmers were class I + II pesticides. 88% (95%CI: 79–94%) of the farmers experienced symptoms of acute poisoning.

50% (n = 44) of the farmers used OPs/CM, 88% of them had self-perceived symptoms, and this was associated with the number (OR = 114, CI 95%, 102–128) and duration of spraying (OR = 2.5, CI 95, 1.1–5.8) and the use of personal protective equipment (OR = 045, CI 95 %, 022–091).

the effects of pesticides on the health of aquatic farmers.

the farmers are at risk of developing symptoms of pesticide poisoning.

the use of pesticides in BCE lake is associated with acute pesticide poisoning among the pesticide applicators, and this is significantly related to their spraying time, and the level of their education and the number of personal protective measures they use.
the farmers are exposed to high levels of pesticide use, and this is associated with a high prevalence of acute symptoms of pesticide poisoning.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

pesticide use in the BCE Lake area is associated with a high number of symptoms of acute pesticide poisonings and that these symptoms are related to the number of hours spraying pesticides, and the level of personal protection used.

the use of OPs/CM pesticides is widespread and associated with a significant number of symptoms among farmers, which can be prevented by using appropriate personal protective equipment and by avoiding the use of the most hazardous pesticides.

the study showed that 1) a large proportion of the farmers had experienced symptoms of OP/CM poisoning, 2) the number of hours the farmers spent spraying with OP/CMs was associated with the risk of experiencing symptoms, and 3) the higher educated farmers reduced the risk of experiencing OP/CM poisoning by adapting additional personal protective measures.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the most important thing to do to prevent pesticide poisoning is to use less toxic pesticides.

there is an urgent need for a comprehensive pesticide management program that includes a ban on the most hazardous pesticides, a pesticide registration system, and training of farmers and pesticide sprayers on safe pesticide management practices.
the farmers in our study were not aware of the health risks associated with pesticide handling.
